text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementBiologyAfter Dinosaurs Died, a Massive Fungus Inherited the ForestsMeet D. rexJCBy Jake Currie12:00 PM CDT on October 15, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleIf you spot a mushroom on a hike, there’s a decent chance it’s from an unknown species. The bulk of most fungi exists unseen as vast networks of tiny threadlike mycelia, only popping their fruiting bodies up to spread their spores. In fact, of the estimated 2-6 million species of fungi on Earth, we’ve only identified around 200,000 of them, a tiny fraction. Now there’s one more to add to the list, and it’s a big one.A team of Chinese mycologists discovered the species after noticing sizable, whitish fruiting bodies near the roots of Chinese cork oak trees located in both subtropical and temperate forests. They appeared to belong to the largest phylum of fungi, ascomycota, which release their spores from sacs rather than producing mushrooms.Read more: “Mushrooms Stole a Trick From Bacteria.
